additions.title: Prompts, cues, and nudges interventions in higher education: a systematic review
additions.abstract: Abstract For over a decade, learning analytics has significantly enhanced understanding and development of learning and teaching processes in higher education. In this setting, prompts, cues, and nudges, among others, have gained attention as specific analytics-informed interventions aimed at influencing learners’ behaviour, engagement, and self-regulation. Prompts and cues primarily stem from educational psychology, while nudges derive from behavioural economics, but all three aim to direct learners towards more effective learning decisions. This paper explores the effectiveness of prompts, cues and nudges, as well as the opportunities and challenges associated with their implementations in higher education. Using a systematic literature review guided by the PRISMA framework, the study synthesizes 39 experimental and quasi-experimental studies reported in 31 papers. The results show that these interventions are implemented across diverse higher education settings and differ in their goals, technological designs, and targeted outcomes. Overall, the evidence suggests positive but domain-specific effects: prompts are most often linked to self-regulation, engagement, and knowledge-related outcomes, cues to cognitive and attentional processes, and nudges to behavioural engagement, while all three are associated with positive outcomes in learning and academic performance. Prompts were the most frequently studied intervention and showed the widest range of measured outcomes. This study also highlights Perceptions and Affective Outcomes as an important but underexplored area for future research across analytics-informed prompts, cues, and nudges. The findings further highlight the importance of experimental and quasi-experimental studies for strengthening evidence in learning analytics research.

additions.title: Learning with GenAI across campuses: student experiences of GenAI-enhanced cybersecurity education
additions.abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly embedded in higher education, yet limited research has examined how GenAI-supported learning operates alongside geographically distributed peer collaboration. This qualitative study explores student experiences in an AI-enhanced cross-campus cybersecurity learning environment connecting university campuses in California, United States, and Ontario, Canada. Anonymous reflections were collected from 19 students (nine in California and ten in Ontario) about their experiences with GenAI-supported learning, cross-campus interaction, associated challenges, and recommendations for improving the learning experience. The findings indicate that students perceived GenAI as supporting concept clarification, greater perceived learning efficiency, idea development, and problem-solving, while also emphasizing the importance of critically evaluating GenAI-generated information. Cross-campus interaction was perceived as exposing students to diverse perspectives, experiences, and approaches to cybersecurity, which participants described as broadening their understanding of collaborative problem-solving across contexts. Students nevertheless identified challenges involving scheduling, technology, differences in experience, GenAI accuracy, and responsible use. They recommended more structured cross-campus projects, hands-on activities, clearer guidance on ethical GenAI use, and greater engagement with industry professionals. The study contributes to research on technology-enhanced learning in higher education by suggesting how GenAI-supported learning and geographically distributed peer interaction can provide complementary educational resources: GenAI offers immediate cognitive and informational support, while cross-campus interaction provides access to situated human perspectives. Together, these experiences highlight the importance of verification, contextual judgment, critical AI literacy, and intentional pedagogical design in GenAI-enhanced learning environments.

additions.title: Curriculum-aligned analysis of assessment feedback: a retrieval-augmented large language model approach for revealing fine-grained student error patterns in higher education
additions.abstract: Abstract Assessment feedback in higher education provides fine-grained evidence about students’ specific errors but remains underutilized as a data source for teaching improvement. This study proposes a method based on a large language model (LLM) that transforms unstructured feedback into curriculum-aligned error analysis in three steps, deriving an error taxonomy from the feedback, mapping each piece to curriculum content by retrieval-augmented generation, and aggregating the annotations into error patterns with quantified cohort coverage. The method was applied to 6072 pieces of feedback across four cohorts (2022–2025) of an undergraduate engineering course. The feedback resolved into recurring, curriculum-aligned error patterns, dominated by missing content and justification, clustered in identifiable modules and weeks, and more than half recurring across cohorts. The resulting annotations achieved 89.1% agreement with human judgment, substantially higher than the 74.7% obtained when an expert-designed taxonomy was applied to the same data. In a focus group, the teaching team confirmed the patterns against their marking experience, proposed course revisions from them, and set the bound that they serve as a reference and not as a direct measure of teaching quality. The study reports a process account of this team’s use of curriculum-aligned error analytics, built on sensemaking and pedagogical response. The analysis turns feedback written for students into evidence on the teaching that preceded it, by which a teaching team can check the alignment between intended outcomes, teaching, and assessment in students’ actual work, reflect on its own practice, and improve its teaching across cohorts.
